The Bushy-tailed jird (Sekeetamys calurus) is a small gerbilline rodent endemic to rocky desert habitats of northeastern Africa and the Middle East. Neonates weigh approximately 4.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 4.5 grams] at birth, a modest mass consistent with the altricial developmental strategy typical of many desert-dwelling murids. The mother provides intensive care during a postpartum nursing period that culminates in weaning, with pups transitioning to nutritional independence at about 30 days after birth [tx = about 30 days after birth] when maintained at a body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This weaning age aligns with values observed in related gerbilline species, though the mass at this milestone, roughly 16.5 grams [Wwx = roughly 16.5 grams], indicates that juveniles have attained a body size that permits independent foraging on seeds and vegetation typical of their arid environment.

Adult body mass in this species shows considerable variation, with the largest recorded individuals reaching an ultimate wet weight of 64 grams [Wwi = 64 grams], a value that places the Bushy-tailed jird among the medium-sized members of the gerbilline radiation. Field surveys and captive colony records indicate that this asymptotic mass is typically achieved within the first several months of life, after which growth decelerates markedly. For individuals raised under standard laboratory conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 23 days [tg = approximately 23 days], a relatively brief interval reflecting the small neonatal mass and the energetic constraints imposed by the demands of lactation in an unpredictable desert environment.

Reproductive output in Sekeetamys calurus is substantial for a rodent of its size. Females produce litters ranging from 1 to 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 1 to 5 pups per litter], and available data from captive breeding colonies indicate that they can sustain approximately 5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 5 litters per year] under favorable conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This high reproductive tempo, combined with a relatively short gestation, allows rapid population turnover in response to ephemeral resource pulses following sporadic rainfall in their native wadi habitats. The maximum recorded reproductive rate thus reflects an opportunistic breeding strategy finely tuned to the stochastic productivity of desert ecosystems.

Sexual maturation in the Bushy-tailed jird occurs relatively early compared to other small mammals of similar body size. Puberty is attained at approximately 70 days after birth [tp = approximately 70 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], a timing that allows young born early in the breeding season to contribute to reproduction within the same year. Correspondingly, metabolic demands during this period are substantial: under thermoneutral conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate reaches 44.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 44.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that supports both sustained growth and the early onset of gonadal activity in this desert-adapted gerbillid.

Longevity in the Bushy-tailed jird is surprisingly extended for a rodent of its size, with the oldest documented individuals reaching a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years] when kept under stable captive conditions at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan considerably exceeds predictions based on body mass alone, suggesting that the species possesses physiological adaptations—such as enhanced resistance to oxidative stress or efficient renal function—that buffer against the harsh conditions of rocky desert environments. The combination of a moderate gestation period, rapid pubertal development, high reproductive output, and extended adult survival delineates a life-history strategy that balances opportunistic reproduction with sustained somatic resilience in an unpredictably arid landscape.
